props.title: The Last Supper

sections.content: The Last Supper (1995) stands as a darkly satirical examination of liberal extremism, following five graduate students who begin murdering conservatives over dinner parties. The film's brilliant premise draws parallels to other politically-charged dark comedies like Dr. Strangelove (1964) and Network (1976), using pitch-black humor to expose ideological fanaticism. Director Stacy Title crafts a wickedly intelligent commentary that feels even more relevant today, with Cameron Diaz, Ron Perlman, and Bill Paxton delivering memorably unsettling performances.

sections.content: The film shares DNA with other morally ambiguous ensemble pieces of the 1990s. Like Reservoir Dogs (1992) and The Usual Suspects (1995), it explores group dynamics under extreme circumstances. The dinner table becomes a stage for ideological warfare, reminiscent of the tense discussions in 12 Angry Men (1957) but with a murderous twist. The gradual ethical deterioration of the characters mirrors similar descents in Lord of the Flies (1963) and A Simple Plan (1998).

The film's exploration of political extremism finds echoes in later works like V for Vendetta (2005) and Sorry to Bother You (2018). Its format of using dinner as a backdrop for tension would later be employed differently but effectively in films like The Invitation (2015) and Get Out (2017), where social gatherings mask sinister intentions. sections.content: The Last Supper helped pave the way for more direct political satires like Thank You for Smoking (2005) and In the Loop (2009). Its blend of horror and political commentary influenced films like God Bless America (2011) and The Hunt (2020), which similarly tackle political division through violent satire. The film's approach to using extreme situations to expose ideological hypocrisy remains influential in contemporary political filmmaking.
